text: In ancient Egypt, strips of papyrus-stalk pith were laid in layers and dried under pressure to form a writing surface. Sheets could be joined into rolls or cut apart for separate use.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Ancient Egyptian scribal kits included water, rush styluses, and cakes of ink. Carbon-based black served ordinary writing; red made with hematite marked emphasis. Reed pens arrived later, in the late first century BCE.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Ancient Egyptian scribes generally began on a papyrus roll’s inner surface, where its fibers ran horizontally, then used the outer surface. Modern terminology calls these surfaces recto and verso.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: For much of ancient Egyptian history, papyrus writing used the cursive hieratic script. Later documents also used demotic, Greek, and Coptic; the writing material did not imply one unchanging script.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Ancient Egyptians used durable strips from papyrus stalks for mats, baskets, ropes, and sandals as well as writing sheets. The same wetland plant supplied both a document surface and everyday manufactured objects.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: From Egypt’s Predynastic period, bundled papyrus stalks formed skiffs for local transport and hunting. Tomb pictures also show the distinctive boat shape in pilgrimage and funeral settings.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Papyrus in Ancient Egypt (2015); https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/papyrus-in-ancient-egypt . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Meketre’s granary model from Thebes, about 1981–1975 BCE, divides storage from an accounting area. The model makes receiving and recording grain a distinct part of the workplace rather than an incidental activity beside the bins.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model of a Granary with Scribes, 20.3.11; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/545281 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.

text: In Meketre’s Theban granary model, dated about 1981–1975 BCE, six sack carriers are accompanied by nine people measuring and accounting. The representation gives unusually visible space to counting the agricultural supply.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model of a Granary with Scribes, 20.3.11; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/545281 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.

text: Meketre’s granary model from Thebes, about 1981–1975 BCE, shows four scribes: two using papyrus rolls and two using wooden writing boards. A single accounting scene depicts more than one writing surface.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model of a Granary with Scribes, 20.3.11; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/545281 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.

text: Meketre’s bakery-and-brewery model from Thebes, about 1981–1975 BCE, groups related grain-processing trades in one complex while giving them separate rooms. The miniature distinguishes shared ingredients from separate workplaces.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model Bakery and Brewery from the Tomb of Meketre, 20.3.12; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/544258 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.

text: In Meketre’s bakery model from Thebes, about 1981–1975 BCE, pestle users precede millers, dough mixers, and oven tenders. The figures represent a sequence of specialized tasks rather than one person performing the whole process.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model Bakery and Brewery from the Tomb of Meketre, 20.3.12; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/544258 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.

text: Meketre’s Theban bakery model, about 1981–1975 BCE, includes conical loaves in a basket and workers shaping other loaves and cakes. Circular stoves and ovens appear together, representing more than one baking arrangement.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Model Bakery and Brewery from the Tomb of Meketre, 20.3.12; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/544258 . Interpretations are explicitly about the model.
